title: Masquerading: Masquerade Account Name
summary: Masquerade account name is the practice of creating a user or service account whose name imitates something the environment already trusts, or of renaming an existing account to that effect. Common patterns are names that match legitimate software service accounts, backup or monitoring identities, container cluster management roles, and generic labels such as admin, help or root; a related pattern is deleting an account and recreating one with the same name so that old references appear consistent. The behaviour is usually a supporting step for persistence or access, and the account is frequently placed in a privileged group at the same time. Detection depends on comparing new account creations and renames against the inventory of accounts that legitimate provisioning creates, and on checking who made the change, from which host, with which privileges, and whether the name duplicates or closely resembles an existing one. Legitimate software installs do create service accounts, so the strongest signals are near duplicates of existing names, reused names shortly after deletion, and accounts of this type that authenticate from unusual sources. This differs from impersonation of a trusted person or organisation, which is about identity rather than account naming.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker creates an account with a name that sounds normal and trusted. An account is a name and password that lets someone use a system. The friendly name makes the account escape notice. Sometimes they only rename an account that already exists.
beginner.whyItMatters: Administrators look for strange account names on a system. A name like backup service or help desk looks familiar. That account can be used later to log in and stay hidden. Attackers often give it extra power at the same time. A boring name is a very cheap disguise.
howItWorks: The attacker creates a new account, or renames one they already control.
They choose a name that copies software service accounts already on the system.
Names that sound official, such as admin or help, are also common.
They may add the account to a powerful group for later use.
They can also delete an account and recreate it with the same name.
Someone reviewing accounts by name sees nothing that looks out of place.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where each person has a named hook for their keys. A stranger adds a key to a new hook labelled flat cleaning. It sounds like a normal job, so nobody asks who put it there or who holds the spare key.
takeaways: Judge an account by its creation, owner and activity, not by its name.
Near duplicates of existing account names are worth investigating.
Watch for a name being reused soon after an account is deleted.
